summary:
We propose HelioGraph-8, an ultra-lightweight (8 kg, 12U CubeSat-scale) solar-plasmonic micro-reactor designed for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) on Mars. Unlike NASA's MOXIE, which requires heavy electrical power and vents carbon monoxide as waste, HelioGraph-8 uses concentrated sunlight and a Titanium Dioxide-Liquid Gallium (TiO₂-Ga) plasmonic catalyst to split Martian CO₂ into breathable Oxygen (O₂) and solid Graphene with zero waste.
To ensure real-world thermal and structural feasibility, the system separates operations into three isolated chambers: (1) a Silica Aerogel-insulated High-Temp Plasmonic Reaction Chamber, (2) a 3D-printed Titanium Micro-Channel Cooling & Graphene Deposition Chamber, and (3) a Low-Temperature Hollow-Fiber Nanoporous O₂ Separation Chamber. Equipped with an electrodynamic dust-shielded Fresnel lens and a self-cleaning liquid-metal catalyst chip, HelioGraph-8 produces 8.0 g/hr of pure O₂ and 3.0 g/hr of solid graphene, while offering direct Earth spin-off applications in zero-fouling solar desalination and non-invasive blood diagnostics.
details:
Terrestrial Analog Site Alignment & NASA Data Integration:
Selecting permanent Moon and Mars base locations depends heavily on local In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) potential—specifically solar irradiance, atmospheric dust levels, and thermal stability. To bridge Earth analog characterization with mission hardware readiness, HelioGraph-8 maps and validates oxygen and graphene production across three primary NASA-studied Martian analogs on Earth:
  • Atacama Desert (Chile): Models hyper-arid conditions, high UV/solar flux, and fine regolith dust attenuation (validating our electrodynamic dust-shield grid).
  • Haughton Crater (Devon Island, Canada): Simulates extreme sub-zero temperatures (-60°C), low solar angles, and impact-fractured basaltic terrain (validating our Silica Aerogel thermal insulation and micro-heater).
  • Mojave Desert / Mars Simulation Chambers (~610 Pa): Tests low-pressure CO2 intake and liquid-gallium plasmonic stability under near-vacuum Martian surface pressures.
By integrating NASA POWER solar irradiance datasets and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) atmospheric dust profiles, our framework evaluates which terrestrial analog sites best replicate future Mars base operational windows, providing a dual-purpose site-characterization and ISRU validation tool.QUICK MISSION METRICS (AT A GLANCE):
  • Total System Mass: 8.0 kg (12U CubeSat Form Factor — 53% lighter than NASA MOXIE)
  • Hourly Output: 8.0 g/hr Pure O₂ + 3.0 g/hr Solid Graphene (Zero Waste)
  • Daily Output (6h Martian Sol): 48.0 g O₂ + 18.0 g Graphene per unit
  • Crew Scalability: 20 modular units (160 kg) produce 960 g/Sol O₂ (114% of one astronaut's daily requirement)
  • Earth Spin-Offs: Zero-fouling solar seawater desalination & non-invasive NIR optical blood diagnostics.
1. Problem Statement & Mission Need:
Sustaining human life on Mars requires a continuous supply of breathable oxygen (O₂), rocket propellant oxidizer, and durable construction materials. Transporting these from Earth is prohibitively expensive. While Mars' atmosphere contains 95% CO₂, existing electrolysis systems consume heavy electrical power and discard carbon as waste gas.
2. Our Solution – The 8 kg HelioGraph-8 Micro-Reactor:
HelioGraph-8 is a compact, rover-mountable (12U CubeSat form factor, 30 × 20 × 20 cm) hybrid reactor that directly converts Martian atmospheric CO₂ into two vital resources: pure O₂ and solid Graphene. By harnessing concentrated solar energy and liquid-metal plasmonic catalysis, it drastically reduces electrical power dependency while achieving zero-waste operation.
3. Three-Chamber System Architecture & Mass Budget (Total: 8.0 kg):
To prevent high-temperature plasma from damaging delicate filtration membranes, our engineering design isolates the process into three thermally decoupled stages:
  • CO₂ Intake & Dust Mitigation (1.2 kg): An electrodynamic dust-shield grid and multi-stage mesh filter prevent Martian dust from clogging the optics, while a miniature diaphragm pump compresses ambient CO₂.
  • Chamber 1 – High-Temp Solar-Plasmonic Reactor (2.2 kg): An acrylic Fresnel concentrator lens (0.16 m²) focuses sunlight onto a TiO₂ + Liquid Gallium plasmonic bowtie catalyst chip. Ultra-lightweight Silica Aerogel thermal insulation contains the intense localized heat without adding heavy ceramic mass.
  • Chamber 2 – Cooling & Graphene Deposition (1.8 kg): Hot reaction products pass through 3D-printed thin-walled titanium micro-cooling channels. Carbon atoms deposit onto a removable composite collector cartridge as solid graphene sheets, while the remaining gas cools down safely.
  • Chamber 3 – Gas Separation & Buffer Storage (1.3 kg): Cooled gas passes through a low-temperature hollow-fiber nanoporous membrane that isolates pure O₂ into a composite-fiber buffer cylinder, ready for astronaut life support or propellant storage.
  • Structural Frame & Avionics (1.5 kg): Lightweight carbon-fiber/aluminum chassis with thermal, pressure, and flow sensors.
4. Catalyst Chip Durability & Lifespan in Martian Conditions:
To ensure the TiO₂ + Liquid Gallium plasmonic chip survives long-term operation in low-pressure, extreme-temperature Martian environments (and Mars simulation test chambers), four key engineering protections are integrated:
  • Anti-Evaporation Protection: A nanoporous TiO₂ overlayer encapsulates the liquid gallium, allowing CO₂ and O₂ molecules to diffuse freely while preventing liquid metal evaporation under Mars' low atmospheric pressure (~610 Pa).
  • Self-Cleaning Liquid Interface (Anti-Coking): Unlike solid catalysts that foul and deactivate when coated by carbon, the liquid gallium surface prevents solid graphene from sticking. Newly formed graphene flakes float on the liquid interface and are continuously swept into Chamber 2 by gas flow.
  • Refractory High-Temp Substrate: The plasmonic bowtie antennas are fabricated on a Silicon Carbide (SiC) / Sapphire substrate, capable of withstanding localized hotspot temperatures above 1,500°C without structural degradation.
  • Nighttime Thermal Stabilization: Combined Silica Aerogel insulation and a low-power resistive micro-heater keep the chip above 30°C during freezing Martian nights (-60°C), ensuring the gallium remains in its active liquid state.
5. Mathematical Model & Performance Calculations:
  • Chemical Stoichiometry: CO₂ (gas) → C (solid graphene) + O₂ (gas)
    (Molar Masses: CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol, C = 12.01 g/mol, O₂ = 32.00 g/mol)
    • Required CO₂ Intake: 0.25 mol/hr × 44.01 g/mol = 11.0 g/hour
    • Pure O₂ Output: 0.25 mol/hr × 32.00 g/mol = 8.0 g/hour (Matches NASA MOXIE's peak rate at less than half the mass)
    • Solid Graphene Yield: 0.25 mol/hr × 12.01 g/mol = 3.0 g/hour
    • Splitting 0.25 mol/hr of CO₂ (ΔH = 393.5 kJ/mol) requires 27.33 Watts of continuous chemical power.
    • Under Martian solar irradiance (590 W/m²), a 0.16 m² (40 × 40 cm) Fresnel lens captures 94.4 Watts of solar power, requiring a 28.9% solar-to-chemical conversion efficiency—achievable via localized plasmonic hotspot amplification.
    • Single 8 kg Unit: Produces 48.0 g of O₂ and 18.0 g of solid graphene per Sol.
    • 20-Unit Modular Array (160 kg total): Produces 960 g (~1 kg) of O₂ per Sol (exceeding one astronaut's daily requirement of 840 g/day) plus 360 g/Sol of graphene for 3D-printed tools, batteries, and radiation shielding.
6. Engineering Risks & Mitigation Strategy:
  • Martian Dust Storm Attenuation: Thick dust storms can reduce solar irradiance by up to 60%. Mitigation: Integrated electrodynamic dust-shield grid clears lenses automatically, while a compact lithium-sulfur battery buffer maintains chip standby heating.
  • Earth Spin-Off Applications (Dual-Use Impact): Beyond Mars, modifying the intake allows solar-driven zero-fouling desalination of seawater (using the non-stick liquid gallium surface to prevent salt scaling) and non-invasive optical blood glucose/hemoglobin diagnostics using low-power Near-Infrared (NIR) plasmonic sensing.
7. Python Yield Simulation Model:
python
# HelioGraph-8: Mars CO2-to-O2 & Graphene Yield Simulator
def simulate_heliograph(solar_hours_per_sol, lens_area_m2=0.16):
mars_solar_irradiance = 590.0 # W/m^2
conversion_efficiency = 0.289 # 28.9% plasmonic efficiency
enthalpy_co2 = 393500.0 # J/mol

solar_power_w = mars_solar_irradiance * lens_area_m2
chem_power_w = solar_power_w * conversion_efficiency
moles_per_hr = (chem_power_w * 3600) / enthalpy_co2

o2_g_hr = moles_per_hr * 32.00
graphene_g_hr = moles_per_hr * 12.01

print(f"Hourly Pure O2: {o2_g_hr:.2f} g/hr | Graphene: {graphene_g_hr:.2f} g/hr")
print(f"Daily O2 ({solar_hours_per_sol}h Sol): {o2_g_hr * solar_hours_per_sol:.2f} g | Graphene: {graphene_g_hr * solar_hours_per_sol:.2f} g")

simulate_heliograph(solar_hours_per_sol=6)
